title: The fletcher (33–34)
hook: the wise straighten the trembling mind as a fletcher straightens an arrow; the mind flaps like a fish on dry land

segments.voice: Yesterday, the racehorse, and your line: awake among the sleeping. Did you find a few quiet minutes before the house woke? Day one hundred sixty-five, and chapter three: thought.

Before factories, arrows were made by hand, one at a time, by a craftsman called a fletcher. The hard part wasn't the feathers or the point. It was the shaft. A length of cane or wood is never quite straight. So the fletcher would warm it gently over a fire, then sight down its length, find the bend, and ease it true, a little at a time, between his hands or in a notched tool. Then sight again. Then ease again. Patient, careful, never snapping it. The Dhammapada says that's exactly what the wise do with something else. Today, verses thirty-three and thirty-four: the fletcher.
screen: `A FLETCHER AT HIS FIRE.` → `SIGHT DOWN THE SHAFT.` → `EASE THE BEND, NEVER SNAP IT.`

segments.voice: Chapter three is called citta, which Müller translates thought. Citta is one of the Pali words for mind: the heart-mind that thinks, feels and wants, all at once. Verse thirty-three: “As a fletcher makes straight his arrow, a wise man makes straight his trembling and unsteady thought, which is difficult to guard, difficult to hold back.” Trembling and unsteady. That's the mind the verse starts with: not a calm mind that needs a little polish, but one that shakes. Verse thirty-four gives the picture: “As a fish taken from his watery home and thrown on the dry ground, our thought trembles all over.” Anyone who's watched a fish on a dock knows that flapping: frantic, desperate, going nowhere. That's the mind when it's pulled out of its old habits: it wants to jump back in. The commentary tells these verses about Meghiya, a monk who was attending the Buddha. He saw a beautiful mango grove and asked to go and meditate there. The Buddha asked him to wait. He asked again, and again, and finally the Buddha let him go. In the grove, Meghiya's mind was flooded with thoughts of desire, anger and harm, and he came back shaken. His mind had flapped like the fish. So the verses don't pretend this is easy. They name the difficulty, and then they give a craft. Not force. The fletcher never snaps the shaft. Warmth, patience, sight down the length, find the bend, ease it true, and sight again. That's also a fair description of the sitting you've been doing for months.
screen: `CITTA — THE HEART-MIND.` · `TREMBLING AND UNSTEADY.` · `A FISH ON DRY GROUND.` · `MEGHIYA IN THE MANGO GROVE.` · then, large: `STRAIGHTEN THE ARROW.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath be the fire that warms the shaft. Now sight down the mind. What's bent in it right now? A worry leaning one way, an irritation pulling another, a plan that won't let go. Pick one bent thought. Don't wrench it. Just see it clearly, and let the next breath ease it a little: less tight, less urgent, closer to true. If it springs back, that's normal. Sight again, ease again. The bell holds the time.
Citta. The mind, or heart-mind: trembling and unsteady at first, and made straight by patient work, like an arrow.
Your line: straighten the arrow. Today, when one thought starts to bend your day, sight down it once and ease it, gently, without snapping. Day one hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Buddhist meditation teachers often use the fletcher image to describe training the mind patiently, and the chapter on citta is commonly taught as the heart of the Dhammapada's teaching on meditation.

match.prompt: match the pictures of chapter three.
pairs: went to the mango grove too soon

myth: the fletcher verse assumes the mind starts out calm
it starts with a mind that is trembling and unsteady, hard to guard.
in the commentary, Meghiya's mind was flooded with troubling thoughts in the mango grove
he went before he was ready and came back shaken.
citta means only the thinking part of the mind
it's the heart-mind: thinking, feeling and wanting together.

fork.setup: you're Meghiya. you see a beautiful mango grove and ask the Buddha if you can go and meditate there. he asks you to wait. what do you do?
options: keep asking until he lets you go.
fork.reveal: Meghiya asked three times and went. in the grove his mind was flooded with desire, anger and harm, and he came back shaken.

original.note: Pali: mind, heart-mind, the title of chapter three.

trapdoor: what you thought: a wise person has a naturally steady mind.
what it means: the wise start with a trembling mind and straighten it patiently, like an arrow.
what a scholar hears: the suttas use citta, mano and vinnana for mind, often nearly interchangeably; the Meghiya episode is also told in the Udana (4.1).

notes: Check Müller's verses 33 and 34 against SBE 10; verse 34 is quoted only up to 'trembles all over'.
Meghiya story (Udana 4.1): asked three times, the Buddha let him go; his mind was assailed by thoughts of sensuality, ill will and harming. Confirm.
The description of how fletchers straightened shafts (warming and easing) is general craft history, kept non-specific.
